title: Locke's Theory of Knowledge
orientation: Russell presents John Locke (1637-1704) as the philosopher of the moderate, successful Revolution of 1688, and as the founder both of philosophical empiricism and of philosophical liberalism. This chapter examines Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding, tracing his case against innate ideas, his account of primary and secondary qualities, his nominalism about universals, and a deep unresolved inconsistency in his theory of knowledge that Russell argues later plagued empiricism through Hume.
historical_background: Locke's father was a Puritan who fought for Parliament. Locke studied at a still-scholastic Oxford, became a physician, and was patronized by Lord Shaftesbury; when Shaftesbury fell from power in 1683 Locke fled with him to Holland, where he remained until the Revolution of 1688. His major works -- the Essay Concerning Human Understanding (finished 1687, published 1690), the Letters on Toleration, the Two Treatises on Government, and Some Thoughts Concerning Education -- were all written or published within a few years of 1688, embodying the Revolution's cautious, successful spirit. Locke's political doctrines, refined by Montesquieu, shaped the American Constitution and, via Voltaire's Lettres philosophiques, influenced eighteenth-century France.
philosophical_problems: Are any ideas or principles innate, or does all knowledge derive from experience?

What is the status of the qualities we perceive in bodies -- are 'primary' qualities (extension, solidity, motion) really in objects while 'secondary' qualities (colour, sound, taste) exist only in the perceiver?
Are general terms and universals (like 'man' or 'body') real features of the world, or merely convenient names for resembling particulars?
If the mind's immediate objects are only its own ideas, how can we have knowledge of an external world or other minds at all?
Can morality be demonstrated with the certainty of mathematics, and what ultimately grounds moral obligation?

philosophers_discussed.name: John Locke
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's sole primary subject: Russell reconstructs his empiricist theory of knowledge -- the rejection of innate ideas, the primary/secondary quality distinction, his nominalism, his account of degrees of assent, and his ultimately inconsistent theory of how ideas relate to an external world -- alongside his hedonistic ethics.

philosophers_discussed.name: René Descartes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as a major influence on the young Locke and as a representative of the rationalist tradition (belief in innate ideas and a priori knowledge) that Locke's empiricism was written against.

philosophers_discussed.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Mentioned as a contemporary rationalist metaphysician whose speculations Locke dismissively called 'this kind of fiddling,' illustrating Locke's impatience with grand metaphysical systems.

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as an opponent of the identification of knowledge with perception (in the Theaetetus) and, with Descartes and the scholastics, as a target of Locke's Book I attack on innate ideas.

philosophers_discussed.name: George Berkeley
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Noted, proleptically, as the philosopher who showed that Locke's arguments for the subjectivity of secondary qualities apply equally to primary qualities, making Locke's dualism 'philosophically out of date.'

philosophers_discussed.name: David Hume
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Referenced as the philosopher who inherited Locke's maxim 'no idea without an antecedent impression' and who tried, more consistently than Locke, to resolve (by dropping external causes of sensation) the very inconsistency Russell diagnoses in Locke.

philosophers_discussed.name: Jeremy Bentham
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Mentioned as Locke's ethical heir, who replaced Locke's theological sanction (heaven and hell) for virtue with the secular mechanism of laws harmonizing private and public interest.

core_concepts.name: Empiricism and the rejection of innate ideas
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke argued the mind starts as 'white paper, void of all characters' and that everything we know comes from experience -- either from the senses (sensation) or from noticing our own mental operations (reflection, or 'internal sense'). Nothing is built in beforehand.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that all our knowledge (with the possible exception of logic and mathematics) is derived from experience; Book I of the Essay argues against Plato, Descartes, and the scholastics that there are no innate ideas or principles, and Book II shows in detail how experience generates our various ideas.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell calls this Locke's 'bold innovation': in Locke's day the mind was widely supposed to know things a priori, so the complete dependence of knowledge on perception was revolutionary, even though it later became part of educated common sense in English-speaking countries.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed across Books I and II of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690), directly opposing the rationalism of Descartes and Leibniz and the scholastic tradition Locke encountered at Oxford.
examples: The 'white paper' (tabula rasa) image for the mind before experience
Locke's two sources of ideas: sensation and reflection on 'the operation of our own mind'
competing_positions: Descartes' and Leibniz's belief in innate ideas and a priori metaphysical knowledge
Plato's Theaetetus, which had argued against identifying knowledge with perception
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became the foundation stone of the British empiricist tradition running through Berkeley and Hume to J. S. Mill.

core_concepts.name: Primary and secondary qualities
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke distinguished qualities that he thought really belong to physical bodies themselves (like shape, solidity, and motion) from qualities that only exist inside the perceiver (like colour, sound, and taste). Without eyes there would be no colours; without ears, no sounds.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Primary qualities -- solidity, extension, figure, motion or rest, and number -- are 'inseparable from body' and actually in bodies; secondary qualities -- colour, sound, smell, and the rest -- exist 'only in the percipient.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as a case where a philosophically mistaken doctrine was nonetheless immensely practically fruitful: it dominated physics (matter-in-motion theories of sound, heat, light, and electricity) until the rise of quantum theory, illustrating that pragmatic usefulness and theoretical truth can come apart.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in Book II of the Essay; grounded in observations such as the effects of jaundice or blue spectacles on colour perception.
examples: Solidity and extension as supposedly objective properties of bodies
objections: Berkeley's demonstration that the same arguments Locke uses against secondary qualities apply equally to primary qualities, since size and shape also vary with the observer's perspective
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Assumed, explicitly or tacitly, by physicists for centuries; refuted in principle by Berkeley but pragmatically useful until modern physics.

core_concepts.name: Nominalism about universals ('Of General Terms')
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Only particular, individual things actually exist in the world. When we use a general word like 'man,' we are not naming some extra abstract thing that all men share -- we are using one particular idea in our minds as a label that applies to many similar particulars.
core_concepts.precise_definition: All things that exist are particulars; general ideas (such as 'man') are applicable to many particulars, but in their own being, as ideas in the mind, they are just as particular as anything else that exists -- their generality consists solely in their applicability to many things.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This 'extreme nominalist position,' extended in Book III's attack on the scholastic doctrine of real 'essence,' cleared away what Russell calls 'metaphysical lumber': it treats species boundaries as made by human classification rather than as fixed in nature, anticipating (though not developing) evolutionary ways of thinking later vindicated by Darwin.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Book III of the Essay, Chapter III ('Of General Terms') and Chapter VI ('Of the Names of Substances').
examples: The general idea 'man' applying to many particular men
Monstrosities/borderline cases used by Locke to show species boundaries are man-made, not natural facts
The scholastic debate over whether the 'essence' of body is extension alone or extension plus solidity, which Locke treats as merely verbal
competing_positions: The scholastic doctrine of real essences fixed in nature
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes this point of view was not generally accepted until Darwin persuaded people to think in terms of gradual, continuous change rather than fixed species.

core_concepts.name: The paradox of ideas: knowledge confined to our own ideas
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke sometimes says the mind can only ever be aware of its own ideas, never of things themselves. But if that is true, how could we ever know that an external world, or other people, actually exist? Locke never really solves this problem, and instead quietly switches to a different, inconsistent account when the first one gets uncomfortable.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Locke states 'the mind ... hath no other immediate object but its own ideas' and that 'knowledge is the perception of the agreement or disagreement of two ideas' -- a view from which it seems to follow that we cannot know of the existence of other people or the physical world, since these, if they exist, are not merely ideas in any mind. Locke escapes this paradox inconsistently, by positing (Book IV, Ch. III) three kinds of 'real' knowledge -- intuitive knowledge of our own existence, demonstrative knowledge of God's existence, and 'sensitive' knowledge of things present to sense -- and by assuming that sensations have external causes which, to some extent, resemble them.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell singles this out as the central defect of Locke's theory of knowledge and traces its consequences forward: the assumption that sensations have resembling external causes cannot itself be justified within strict empiricist principles, and this unresolved difficulty 'troubled empiricism down to the present day,' reappearing in Hume's maxim 'no idea without an antecedent impression.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Book IV of the Essay, especially Chapters I, III, and IV.
examples: Locke's three kinds of knowledge of real existence: intuitive (of ourselves), demonstrative (of God), sensitive (of things present to sense)
Locke's claim that simple ideas must 'agree with things' because the mind cannot invent them on its own
objections: Russell's central charge: Locke escapes the paradox 'by means of an inconsistency so gross that only his resolute adherence to common sense could have made him blind to it'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Hume inherited the difficulty and 'got rid of it' only by dropping the assumption that sensations have external causes -- though Russell notes Hume kept smuggling that assumption back in.

core_concepts.name: Locke's hedonistic ethics and the ideal of prudence
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke thought that, deep down, everyone always acts from a desire for their own pleasure or happiness. Things are called 'good' only because they cause pleasure or reduce pain. Since people who behave virtuously are rewarded in heaven and the wicked punished in hell, being virtuous is ultimately just being sensible, or 'prudent,' about one's own long-term happiness.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Locke holds that 'things are good or evil only in relation to pleasure or pain' and that happiness alone moves desire; virtue is grounded in the rational, self-interested pursuit of one's greatest long-run pleasure, underwritten by divine reward and punishment in an afterlife, so that prudence becomes, in effect, the master virtue.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell reads this as anticipating Bentham's utilitarianism, and connects Locke's stress on prudence to the psychology of Protestant capitalism -- 'the prudent became rich while the imprudent became or remained poor' -- and to a broader liberal belief in the harmony of private and public interest.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Book II, Chapter XX of the Essay.
examples: The hesitant sinner who avoids highway robbery for fear of the 'Divine Magistrate' even if he could escape human law
Discounting of future pleasure, illustrated by people who postpone visiting the dentist
objections: Russell's objection that desire, not pleasure, generally comes first: 'the pleasure is due to the desire, not the desire to the pleasure'
Locke's own admission that men habitually prefer a smaller present pleasure to a greater future one, which strains his claim that all action aims at maximum pleasure
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly anticipates Bentham, who substituted the human lawgiver for God as the mechanism reconciling private and public interest.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Locke's ethics rests on belief in heavenly reward and hellish punishment; Bentham later secularized the same structure through law.

arguments.title: The argument against innate ideas
premises: If we examine the mind before any experience, we find it is like 'white paper, void of all characters, without any ideas.'
All the materials of reason and knowledge that the mind eventually possesses can be traced to experience -- sensation and reflection.
No feature of our actual knowledge requires us to posit ideas or principles present in the mind prior to experience.
arguments.conclusion: There are no innate ideas or principles; all knowledge (excepting perhaps logic and mathematics) is derived from experience.
arguments.explanation: Locke opens the Essay by directly opposing Plato, Descartes, and the scholastics, who held that the mind possesses certain truths (such as principles of logic, or the idea of God) independently of experience. Russell notes this seemed almost a truism to later readers but was, in Locke's day, 'a new and revolutionary doctrine,' since 'from [Plato's] time onwards almost all philosophers, down to and including Descartes and Leibniz, had taught that much of our most valuable knowledge is not derived from experience.'
implications: Grounds the entire empiricist program of Books II-IV of the Essay
Sets up the later tension over how ideas relate to an external, mind-independent world

arguments.title: The primary/secondary quality distinction
premises: Certain qualities (colour, taste, sound, smell) vary or disappear depending on the state of the perceiver (e.g., jaundice makes things look yellow; blue spectacles tint everything blue).
Other qualities (solidity, extension, figure, motion, number) appear to remain constant properties of a body regardless of who perceives it or how.
arguments.conclusion: Secondary qualities exist only in the perceiving mind, while primary qualities are actually in bodies themselves.
arguments.explanation: Locke has, Russell says, 'good grounds' for treating secondary qualities as subjective, citing cases like jaundice. But he does not apply the same reasoning to qualities like extension or motion, which likewise appear different depending on perspective (near vs. far, fast vs. slow to different observers).
objections: Berkeley later showed the same style of argument used against secondary qualities equally undermines the supposed objectivity of primary qualities, since these too vary with observation conditions.
implications: Berkeley's rebuttal made Locke's dualism 'philosophically out of date,' even though it remained pragmatically central to physics for centuries.

arguments.title: Locke's inconsistent escape from the paradox of ideas
premises: Locke's official epistemology states that 'knowledge is the perception of the agreement or disagreement of two ideas,' and that the mind's 'immediate object' is only its own ideas.
If this were strictly true, we could never know of the existence of anything beyond our own ideas -- not other people, not the physical world.
Locke finds this consequence paradoxical and unacceptable to common sense.
arguments.conclusion: Locke instead asserts, inconsistently, that we have three genuine kinds of knowledge of real existence (of ourselves, of God, and of things present to sense) and that our sensations must have external causes resembling them -- without ever justifying this from his own empiricist premises.
arguments.explanation: Russell argues that the assumption sensations have resembling external causes 'is one which, if maintained, must be maintained on grounds wholly independent of experience,' since we experience only the sensations, never their supposed causes. Locke's 'resolute adherence to common sense' let him overlook this gross inconsistency, which Russell regards as the deepest flaw in Locke's theory of knowledge.
objections: Russell's own objection, stated at length, that the move is simply inconsistent with Locke's official definition of knowledge
implications: The same unresolved problem reappears in Hume, whose maxim 'no idea without an antecedent impression' only seems plausible if impressions are assumed (against strict empiricism) to have outside causes.

arguments.title: The claim that morality is capable of demonstration
premises: We have clear ideas of a Supreme Being and of ourselves as rational, understanding beings.
From self-evident propositions about these ideas, necessary consequences can in principle be drawn with the certainty of mathematics.

Example propositions, such as 'where there is no property, there is no injustice,' seem to follow merely from the definitions of the terms involved, 'as certainly ... as that a triangle has three angles equal to two right ones.'
arguments.conclusion: Morality could, in principle, be placed 'among the sciences capable of demonstration,' comparable to mathematics.
arguments.explanation: Russell finds this passage 'puzzling,' since it wavers between making moral rules dependent on God's decrees and treating them as analytic truths following merely from definitions; moreover, the example propositions Locke offers do not obviously look like ethical claims at all.
objections: Russell notes Locke never explains what antecedent concept of goodness could justify or explain why God's decrees take the particular form they do, rather than some other.
The worked examples Locke gives seem definitional rather than genuinely ethical.
implications: Illustrates the tension in Locke's ethics between rationalist ambition (demonstrable morality) and his actual hedonistic, theologically grounded account of moral motivation.

key_distinctions: Sensation vs. reflection ('internal sense') as sources of ideas
Credibility vs. consistency as competing philosophical virtues
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Locke writes against Plato's Theaetetus (which opposed identifying knowledge with perception), against Descartes' rationalism (by which Locke was nonetheless influenced as a young man), and against scholasticism's doctrine of real essences, all targeted by his rejection of innate ideas and his nominalism about universals.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Berkeley extends Locke's empiricism to attack the primary/secondary quality distinction itself; Hume inherits and radicalizes Locke's empiricism, taking over 'no idea without an antecedent impression' while inheriting the same unresolved problem of how ideas connect to an external world; Bentham develops Locke's hedonistic, prudence-centred ethics into a secular utilitarianism.
political_social_context: Locke wrote the Essay during the years before 1688 when, as a Shaftesbury client in exile, he could not safely participate in English politics; Russell stresses that Locke's theoretical caution and anti-dogmatism -- 'wherever his doctrines differ from those of his forerunners, they are to the effect that truth is hard to ascertain' -- is intimately connected to the toleration, parliamentary gradualism, and laissez-faire temper of the liberal movement he founded.
religion_science_culture_context: Locke was a devout Christian who accepted revelation as a genuine source of knowledge but insisted, in his chapter 'Of Enthusiasm,' that 'revelation must be judged by reason,' opposing the claims of religious sects to unmediated personal revelation; his primary/secondary quality distinction also shaped physics until the rise of quantum theory.
russell_presentation: Russell presents Locke as philosophy's luckiest figure: he completed his theoretical masterpiece just as England's government fell into the hands of men who shared his political outlook, so both his sound views and his errors (like the primary/secondary quality distinction) proved historically fruitful. Russell stresses Locke's 'sensible' and undogmatic temperament -- he 'is always willing to sacrifice logic rather than become paradoxical' -- as both his great practical virtue and his central theoretical weakness, since Locke's principles, followed out rigorously, would lead to conclusions he refuses to draw. Russell traces Locke's empiricism from the rejection of innate ideas, through the theory of primary and secondary qualities, to an extreme nominalism about universals, before identifying what he regards as the decisive flaw: Locke's official view that we know only our own ideas is incompatible with his common-sense insistence that we know an external, causally connected world, and he resolves this by sheer inconsistency rather than argument. Russell closes by examining Locke's hedonistic ethics (pleasure as the sole spring of action, underwritten by divine reward and punishment) as an anticipation of Bentham, while criticizing its central claim that 'we only desire pleasure' as psychologically the wrong way round.
critical_context: Common scholarly assessment, which Russell shares: a philosophy that is fully self-consistent (like some rationalist systems) can nonetheless be wholly false, while one riddled with inconsistencies, like Locke's, can still be 'partially true' -- Russell explicitly argues there is 'no reason to suppose that a self-consistent system contains more truth than one which, like Locke's, is obviously more or less wrong,' a methodological remark that has itself been debated by later historians of philosophy weighing coherence against plausibility as theoretical virtues.
key_takeaways: Locke founded both empiricism (all knowledge derives from experience) and philosophical liberalism, and his theoretical work and the political victory of 1688 reinforced each other historically.
Locke's rejection of innate ideas made perception 'the first step and degree towards knowledge,' a revolutionary claim in his time.
The primary/secondary quality distinction was philosophically refuted by Berkeley but remained practically central to physics for centuries.
Locke's nominalism treats species and essences as verbal/classificatory rather than fixed in nature, anticipating (without developing) evolutionary thinking.
Locke's claim that the mind knows only its own ideas is inconsistent with his common-sense assumption that sensations have resembling external causes -- a problem Russell traces forward into Hume.

Locke's hedonistic, theologically grounded ethics ('we only desire pleasure') anticipates Bentham's utilitarianism but is vulnerable to the objection that desire generally precedes and explains pleasure, not the reverse.
study_notes:
The key to reading this chapter is to hold two of Russell's judgments about Locke together at once: Locke is philosophy's most practically successful thinker, and Locke is, strictly, an inconsistent thinker. These are not in tension for Russell -- they are the same fact seen from two angles. Locke refuses to follow his own premises to uncomfortable conclusions, which makes him a poor logician but gives his philosophy remarkable staying power, because common sense rarely tolerates the 'strange consequences' that rigorous system-building produces.

Track the chapter's central problem carefully: if, as Locke says, the mind's only immediate objects are its own ideas, then strictly we can never get outside our ideas to check whether they correspond to an external world. Locke wants this correspondence (sensations caused by, and resembling, real physical objects) but cannot derive it from his own principles. Watch how this same fault line reopens in Berkeley (who denies matter to remove the puzzle) and Hume (who tries to do without external causes altogether) -- the three chapters on Locke, Berkeley, and Hume in this book form a single connected argument about where consistent empiricism leads.

Finally, notice Russell's methodological aside about consistency versus credibility: a perfectly logical system can still be false in its premises, while a messy, common-sensical philosophy like Locke's can still capture more truth precisely because it keeps bumping up against facts that a tidier system would have to deny.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Locke's image for the mind before any experience: a blank sheet with nothing written on it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine that the mind, prior to experience, has no innate ideas or principles, and is furnished entirely by sensation and reflection.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Properties like shape, solidity, and motion that Locke thought really belong to objects themselves.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Qualities Locke defines as 'inseparable from body': solidity, extension, figure, motion or rest, and number.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Properties like colour, sound, and taste that Locke thought exist only in the mind of the perceiver, not in objects themselves.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: All perceivable qualities other than the primary ones -- colour, sound, smell, taste, etc. -- which Locke holds are 'only in the percipient.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Noticing your own mind at work -- thinking, doubting, believing -- as a second source of ideas alongside the five senses.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Locke's second source of simple ideas, alongside sensation: perception of the operations of one's own mind.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The 'nominal essence' of a thing is just how we define the word for it; the 'real essence' is its actual, often unknown, physical makeup.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Locke's distinction, in Book III of the Essay, between the verbal definition attached to a general term (nominal essence) and a thing's unknown underlying physical constitution (real essence), used to dissolve the scholastic doctrine of essence.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: In Locke's day, this meant claiming to have a personal, direct revelation from God -- not excitement as we use the word today.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Locke's term, discussed in his chapter 'Of Enthusiasm,' for unwarranted claims of personal revelation, which he regards as undermining rational, social truth-seeking and as flattering 'men's laziness, ignorance, and vanity.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The reasons we have for believing something is likely true, even without certainty -- mainly, either our own experience or the reliable testimony of others.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Locke's term for the basis of 'degrees of assent': conformity with our own experience, or the testimony of others' experience.

questions.prompt: What does Locke mean by describing the mind, prior to experience, as 'white paper'?
questions.answer: That the mind has no innate ideas or principles at birth; all its content is supplied by later experience (sensation and reflection).
questions.explanation: This is Locke's central image for rejecting innatism, opening Book II of the Essay.

questions.prompt: According to Locke, what are the two sources from which all our ideas are derived?
questions.answer: Sensation (the external senses) and reflection, or 'internal sense' (perception of the operations of our own mind).
questions.explanation: Together these two sources are meant to account for the entire content of human knowledge without any innate contribution.

questions.prompt: Which later philosopher pointed out that Locke's arguments for the subjectivity of secondary qualities (like colour) apply equally to primary qualities (like extension)?
questions.explanation: Russell notes that 'ever since Berkeley, Locke's dualism on this point has been philosophically out of date,' even though it remained practically useful in physics.

questions.prompt: Contrast Locke's claim that 'knowledge is the perception of the agreement or disagreement of two ideas' with his later claim that we have sensitive knowledge of things present to sense. Why does Russell see these as inconsistent?
questions.answer: The first claim implies the mind can only ever know its own ideas, never anything external to them -- so strictly we could not know external objects or other minds exist. The second claim assumes we do have genuine knowledge of an external world causing our sensations. Russell argues Locke never reconciles these, and simply switches between them as convenient.
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's central philosophical crux, which Russell calls an inconsistency 'so gross that only his resolute adherence to common sense could have made him blind to it.'

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Locke's argument against innate ideas in his own basic terms.
questions.answer: If ideas were innate, the mind before experience would already contain some content; but examining the mind before experience shows it to be like blank paper; all the ideas and knowledge we do have can be traced to sensation or reflection; therefore there is no need to posit, and no evidence for, innate ideas or principles.
questions.explanation: This argument opens the Essay and sets up the entire empiricist program that follows in Books II-IV.

questions.prompt: How does Locke's ethical hedonism explain why a naturally violent or dishonest man might nonetheless act virtuously?
questions.answer: Because Locke ties virtue to the rational pursuit of one's own long-run happiness: since God punishes vice and rewards virtue in the afterlife, a prudent person will restrain wicked impulses out of self-interested calculation, even without fear of earthly punishment.
questions.explanation: Russell illustrates this with Locke's image of a would-be highwayman deterred by fear of the 'Divine Magistrate.'

questions.prompt: How does Russell compare the theoretical virtue of internal consistency with the practical virtue of credibility, using Locke as his example?
questions.answer: Russell argues a fully self-consistent philosophy can still be wholly false, while an inconsistent philosophy, like Locke's, can be more nearly true precisely because its inconsistencies let it stay closer to observed fact and common sense, rather than following false premises rigorously to absurd conclusions.
questions.explanation: Russell states there is 'no reason to suppose that a self-consistent system contains more truth than one which, like Locke's, is obviously more or less wrong.'

flashcards.back: The view that the mind is blank ('white paper') prior to experience, with all ideas ultimately derived from sensation and reflection.

flashcards.front: Name Locke's two sources of ideas.
flashcards.back: Sensation (external senses) and reflection ('internal sense,' perception of our own mind's operations).
Solidity, extension, figure, motion or rest, and number.

flashcards.front: List examples of Locke's secondary qualities.
flashcards.back: Colour, sound, smell, taste -- qualities Locke holds exist only in the perceiver.

flashcards.front: Who showed that Locke's argument against the objectivity of secondary qualities also undermines primary qualities?

flashcards.back: Claiming a personal, direct revelation from God -- a religious, not emotional, term in Locke's usage.
Conformity with our own experience, and the testimony of others' experience.

flashcards.front: What is Locke's central, unresolved inconsistency according to Russell?
flashcards.back: Locke claims knowledge is only of our own ideas, yet also assumes our sensations have external causes resembling them -- a claim his own empiricism cannot justify.

flashcards.front: What are Locke's three kinds of knowledge of real existence?
flashcards.back: Intuitive knowledge of our own existence, demonstrative knowledge of God's existence, and sensitive knowledge of things present to sense.

flashcards.front: According to Locke, what alone moves human desire?
flashcards.back: Happiness/pleasure -- 'What is it moves desire? I answer, happiness, and that alone.'

flashcards.front: What is Russell's objection to Locke's claim that we only desire pleasure?
flashcards.back: Russell argues this puts the cart before the horse: as a rule, pleasure results from getting what we desire, rather than desire being caused by anticipated pleasure.

flashcards.front: Who did Locke later ethically anticipate, according to Russell?
flashcards.back: Jeremy Bentham, though Bentham replaced God's rewards/punishments with the mechanism of human law.

flashcards.front: What nominalist claim does Locke make in Book III's 'Of General Terms'?
flashcards.back: All that exists is particular; general ideas like 'man' are particular ideas that apply, by resemblance, to many things -- their generality is not a feature of the world itself.

flashcards.front: What historical event does Russell say Locke 'faithfully embodies'?
flashcards.back: The Revolution of 1688, the 'most moderate and most successful of all revolutions.'

Clear explanation of why Russell sees them as inconsistent
Engagement with Russell's broader claim about consistency vs. credibility
